title: The ages (Avot 5:21)
hookLine: five for Scripture, ten for Mishnah, thirteen for mitzvot, and on to old age
tomorrow: Saba stands up when an older friend walks in. why bother, at eighty?

lines: THE CANDLES ARE A FIRE HAZARD.
cards: The cake is out, the candles are a fire hazard, and the whole family is singing slightly off key.
The grandfather at the head of the table, Saba to the kids, blows, laughs, and says the thing people say at birthdays like this: well, what's left for me now? Crossword puzzles? Everyone laughs.
It's a joke. Mostly. But there's an old answer to his question, in the Mishnah, and it doesn't say crossword puzzles.
It gives every age a job, from five years old to a hundred, and eighty's job might surprise him.

teach.b: It's in Pirkei Avot, from a sage named Yehuda ben Tema. At five, he says, Scripture. At ten, Mishnah.
At thirteen, the commandments: that's the age of a bar mitzvah. At fifteen, Talmud. At eighteen, the chuppah, the wedding canopy.
At forty, understanding. At fifty, counsel, the age to give advice. At sixty, old age.
And at eighty: gevurah. Strength, the deep kind, the kind that's left when the easy strength is gone. Listen to the shape of it.
Childhood is for taking in. The middle years are for building. And the later years aren't blank pages.

Counsel, understanding, a gray head people look to, and at eighty, a strength of its own. The last lines get quiet: ninety, for bending low; a hundred, as if already passed from the world. The Mishnah doesn't pretend.
But it never says any age is for nothing.

So when the man at eighty asks what's left, the old answer is: something only an eighty-year-old can do. Something to tell a friend tonight: in the Mishnah's list of life's ages, eighty is the age of strength.

how: Yehuda ben Tema's list of the ages is studied with the rest of Pirkei Avot, which some communities read on Shabbat afternoons between Passover and Rosh Hashanah.

o: the eras of Jewish history, from Abraham onward
the stages of a life, each with its own task
the years when Jewish holidays were first kept

games.q: the ages, and their tasks — tap the pairs.

s: the Mishnah's list of ages stops at sixty
it goes on: seventy, gray hair; eighty, strength; and on to ninety and a hundred.
in Avot 5:21, thirteen is the age for the commandments
the same age as a bar mitzvah.
Yehuda ben Tema calls old age a time with nothing left to do
fifty is for counsel, sixty old age, seventy gray hair, eighty strength. no age is for nothing.

games.q: your great-aunt, recently retired, sighs: "I'm not useful to anyone anymore." what does Yehuda ben Tema's list offer her?
o: her age has a task of its own: counsel, understanding, a strength others lean on.
she's earned the right to rest, since later life is for stepping back.
age doesn't matter at all; she should act like she's thirty again.
games.why: the list gives the later years counsel, understanding, gray hair people look to, and at eighty, gevurah: strength.

practice: Look at one thing that shows time passing: an old photo, a birthday card, or just the backs of your own hands. Ask what this stage of your life is for, the one you're in right now.
Let one task come to mind, and say its name quietly.

wordCard.voice: The ages: Yehuda ben Tema's map of a life in Pirkei Avot, from Scripture at five to strength at eighty and beyond.

orig.note: Hebrew: strength, might. Avot 5:21: at eighty, for gevurah.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: every age has its task, and eighty's is strength. Happy birthday to whoever's turning anything.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 5:21 (Yehuda ben Tema: the ages, from five for Scripture to a hundred)
